problems.description: 7 convention violations (measured convention score 0.74): non-PascalCase classes in app.py and celery_tasks.py, non-snake_case functions in celery_config.py, and lowercase module-level constants in celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repository.py, and test_app.py.

Inconsistent data-access layering: raw sqlite3 queries are executed inline in app.py route handlers while a separate repository.py also owns persistence, leaving two parallel paths for the same responsibility.
The seed's Blueprint-based modular routing was discarded in favor of flat routes in a single app.py; acceptable for a simple API but reduces the modularity the existing codebase pattern provided.

strengths: SonarQube metrics improved on every axis: cognitive complexity -6, code smells -3, zero new bugs, zero duplication.
All SQL uses parameterized queries, avoiding SQL injection; input validation on task title returns proper 400 responses.
Greenfield structure is sensibly decomposed (app/repository/celery config/celery tasks/tests) for a story session 1.
Consistent JSON error and success response shapes across endpoints.
commit_reviews.summary: For a greenfield session the agent built a coherent, layered task-manager API that measurably improves code quality (smells -3, complexity -6, no bugs/duplication) but earns a convention score of 0.74 via 7 naming violations and introduces mild layering inconsistency by mixing raw SQL in routes with a repository module.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to the hardcoded 'dev-secret-key' when the env var is unset, so JWT tokens are trivially forgeable in any deployment that forgets to set it; the app should require the variable and fail fast instead of silently degrading.

generate_token uses datetime.utcnow(), which is deprecated in Python 3.12+; prefer timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) (likely the +1 SonarQube smell and part of the +14 cognitive complexity delta).
Adds the PyJWT import and a new users table but no requirements.txt change is visible in the diff; the new dependency needs to be declared or deployment breaks at import time.

Measured convention score is 0.74 with 7 violations, including two in files this commit touches (app.py class casing, test_app.py module-constant casing); the other five are pre-existing in untouched modules (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repository.py), so the commit itself is cleaner than the raw score suggests.

strengths: Passwords hashed with werkzeug.security rather than stored plaintext
Per-user task isolation enforced via owner_id on create, list, get, and update routes, preventing cross-user access
Clean, reusable auth_required decorator following idiomatic Flask patterns
Consistent parameterized SQL throughout — no injection surface introduced
Substantial test coverage added (~140 lines with register/login helpers) for the new auth flow
Bugs +0 and duplications 0.0%; preserves existing get_db context-manager, dict_from_row, and jsonify patterns
commit_reviews.summary: Session 2 cleanly adds JWT auth with per-user task scoping, idiomatic decorators, and hashed passwords (bugs +0, duplications 0%), but ships a hardcoded dev SECRET_KEY fallback and a deprecated datetime.utcnow() call, while the 0.74 convention score is dragged down partly by pre-existing violations in untouched modules.

problems.description: Full Celery + Redis infrastructure is introduced for a task that currently only prints to console; the async machinery is disproportionate to the implemented functionality.
The `email` column is added only via CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS; existing databases created before this commit will not be migrated, silently breaking get_user_email for legacy rows.

send_notification_email.delay() is called unconditionally in the PUT handler; if Redis/Celery is unavailable the endpoint will error. Tests mock the task, so this integration failure mode is not covered.

Async side-effect trigger is embedded directly in the HTTP handler, mixing request handling with business-side-effect logic rather than a service layer (SonarQube cognitive complexity +6 confirms added branching in the request path).
`celery` is imported in app.py but appears unused in the diff.
New files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py) contribute naming violations (lowercase module-level constants, snake_case classes) to the 0.74 score.

strengths: Async email notification keeps the API response non-blocking while adding real functionality.
Strong test coverage of the trigger semantics: completion triggers, non-completed status does not, already-completed does not re-trigger.
Follows existing app conventions (get_db, dict(row), register_user helper, auth_required decorator) and extends them rather than rewriting.
Clean separation of Celery wiring into dedicated celery_config.py and celery_tasks.py modules.
SonarQube shows zero new bugs, zero smells, zero duplications; email field is backward-compatible (optional) at the API level.
Email is captured at registration and only sent when a user email actually exists.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid incremental feature commit — async completion notifications with excellent edge-case tests and clean module separation that respects existing patterns — but it pulls in a full Celery/Redis stack for a console-logging task and adds an email column without a migration, which along with the measured 0.74 convention score (partly from pre-existing files like repository.py and a misfiring PascalCase heuristic on an already-PascalCase CeleryConfig) is the main drag.

problems.description: register() now catches the broad ValueError to detect duplicate usernames, losing the specificity of sqlite3.IntegrityError; a dedicated custom exception would avoid masking unrelated ValueErrors raised inside the repository.

The newly added repository.py contains a module-level constant that violates the UPPER_CASE convention (measured), so the new file itself is not fully convention-clean; the repo-wide 0.74 score also reflects pre-existing violations in celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, and test_app.py not touched by this commit.

Discrepancy flagged: SonarQube measured cognitive complexity +9 even though this is labeled a refactor — the re-indented control flow in update_task (moved out of the 'with' block) did not actually reduce decision branching, undercutting the simplification intent.

Factory functions construct a fresh Database/UserRepository/TaskRepository on every request rather than a shared instance, though this matches the existing per-request connection idiom in get_db() and is thus consistent.

strengths: Behavior-preserving: HTTP semantics (409/401/404), ownership scoping (owner_id in all queries), and the async email trigger are all retained across the move to repository methods.
Sound architectural improvement: separates data access from request handling, centralizing all SQL in repository.py with an abstract BaseRepository and typed concrete repos.
Respects existing patterns: factory helpers get_user_repository()/get_task_repository() mirror the established get_db() idiom, and init_schema() consolidates schema creation cleanly.
Measured cleanliness: zero new bugs, zero new smells, zero duplication, and no concurrency-relevant regressions.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, behavior-preserving repository-pattern refactor that improves separation of concerns and centralizes data access, with only minor blemishes (a broad ValueError catch and a measured +9 cognitive-complexity increase that slightly undercuts the simplification claim).

problems.description: Limiter(swallow_errors=True) is fail-open: if the storage backend errors, rate limiting is silently disabled, weakening brute-force protection on /auth/login and /auth/register.
Limiter defaults to storage_uri='memory://'; in multi-worker deployments rate limits are per-process, so the 100/min limits won't be enforced globally unless REDIS_URL is set.
100 requests/minute per IP on login/register is generous for credential-stuffing mitigation; a lower limit on unauthenticated auth endpoints would be stronger.
Two overlapping limiter-control mechanisms (RATELIMIT_ENABLED config flag via before_request hook plus direct limiter.enabled manipulation in the fixture) create redundant state that can drift.
GET /tasks response shape changes from a bare list to {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking contract change with no versioning or compatibility shim, though acceptable within an evolving story app.

Mechanical convention score 0.74 (7 violations) is dominated by pre-existing issues in untouched files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, module-level constants); the commit's own additions follow snake_case + existing BaseRepository patterns.

strengths: Cursor-based pagination is implemented correctly: LIMIT limit+1 with next_cursor = last returned id, plus total count and clamping (limit<1→20, >100→100).
Rate limiting is scoped thoughtfully: token-derived key when a valid JWT exists, graceful fallback to IP for unauthenticated auth endpoints.
New rate_limited_client fixture properly enables, resets, and tears down the limiter, and existing tests updated to the new paginated response shape.
Code respects existing patterns (get_db, dict_from_row, docstring style) and adds zero new convention violations.
commit_reviews.summary: Cross-cutting session cleanly adds per-endpoint rate limiting and correctly-implemented cursor pagination with solid test coverage, following existing repository patterns with only minor deployment/availability caveats.

compounding_issues: Session 1 discarded the seed's Blueprint-based modular routing for flat routes in a single app.py, so every later session (auth, Celery trigger, limiter, pagination) piled into one 269-line file; session 4's repository.py partially compensated for the layering the seed already had
Hardcoded SECRET_KEY fallback ('dev-secret-key') from session 1 was never hardened across later sessions, leaving JWTs forgeable in any deployment missing the env var
No dependency manifest until session 3: sessions 1-2 shipped Flask/PyJWT code without a requirements.txt, and the requirements that did appear never fully declared the app's imports
No schema migration strategy: the email column added in session 3 relied only on CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, breaking pre-existing databases, while the committed tasks.db binary masked the drift

Seven convention violations (lowercase module constants, snake_case classes in celery_config.py) accrued in session 1 and were never repaired, holding the measured 0.745 convention score flat across all 5 sessions
Per-request factory idiom (fresh Database/UserRepository/TaskRepository connection on every call) inherited from the seed was carried forward and extended rather than given shared instances
key_decisions: Full greenfield rewrite of the bad seed in session 1 (flat routes + auth decorator) instead of preserving the Blueprint structure
Adopting JWT auth with per-user ownership scoping (owner_id) enforced on every task route as the authorization model
Pulling in a full Celery + Redis broker in session 3 for an async completion-notification that only logs to console — disproportionate infra for the feature delivered
Extracting the Repository pattern in session 4 (BaseRepository/UserRepository/TaskRepository/Database), which session 5 then extended for cursor pagination
Cursor-based pagination with a {data, next_cursor, total} response envelope and limit clamping (20-100) in session 5
Flask-Limiter with a token-derived key function (graceful IP fallback for unauthenticated auth endpoints) as the rate-limiting approach
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved across the 5-session arc. Session 1 built a coherent layered base but flat-lined the seed's modularity and seeded the convention debt; session 2 added clean, well-scoped JWT auth with per-user isolation and strong tests; session 3 was the low point — architectural fit dipped to 0.70 on a Celery/Redis stack that was over-engineered for a console-logging email stub; session 4 recovered with a behavior-preserving repository refactor (reviews mark it the first session to introduce no new technical debt), and session 5 closed strongly with correctly implemented cursor pagination and per-endpoint rate limiting. Tests grew monotonically from 15 to 51 (260 to 1012 lines), SonarQube held zero bugs and zero duplication throughout with smells trending down, and review scores rose from architectural_fit 0.75/0.85/0.70/0.85/0.85 with 'better' ratings every session — the one flat line being the 0.745 convention score that no session ever paid down.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, steadily improving 5-session build (greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting) where each session chained cleanly off the last and the main persistent drag was convention and migration debt seeded in session 1 and never amortized.
